html:
Teotihuacan was a huge planned city in the Valley of Mexico, about 40 km northeast of modern Mexico City, that flourished from about 100 BCE to about 550 CE. At its height it held perhaps 100,000 people and was the largest city in the Americas.

The city was laid out on a grid along the Avenue of the Dead. At its sides stand the Pyramid of the Sun, the Pyramid of the Moon and the Temple of the Feathered Serpent. Most people lived in large stone apartment compounds shared by several families, some housing migrants from other regions. Walls were covered in bright murals.

Its wealth came partly from obsidian, the volcanic glass used for blades, which its workshops traded across Mesoamerica. Its reach went much further than trade. In 378 CE a man from Teotihuacan arrived at the Maya city of Tikal, and a new king with Teotihuacan links took the throne (see Teotihuacan intervenes at Tikal).

Much is unknown. We do not know the language its people spoke, or the names of its rulers; there are no royal portraits or tombs, which may mean it was ruled by a council. Around 550 the centre was burned, perhaps in an uprising, and the city shrank. Centuries later the Aztecs found the ruins and named them Teotihuacan, "the place where the gods were born".
